before.content_html:
More Than a Wash

For a Roman citizen living in a busy city such as Pompeii, Herculaneum or Rome itself, the public thermae (baths) were one of the most important buildings in daily life. Going to the baths was not simply about getting clean. Romans visited in the afternoon after work, spending hours exercising, socialising, conducting business and relaxing. Admission was cheap — sometimes free on special occasions sponsored by a local politician — so the baths were genuinely open to people from many social backgrounds, though men and women were usually separated, either by bathing at different times or in different sections.

Key Fact

A typical bath complex was organised in a sequence of rooms: the apodyterium (changing room), the tepidarium (warm room), the caldarium (hot room) and the frigidarium (cold room/cold plunge pool). Bathers moved through these rooms to cleanse their skin and relax their muscles.

The Prescribed Source: The Forum Baths, Pompeii

The Forum Baths at Pompeii are among the best-preserved bath buildings in the Roman world. The complex lies close to the civic centre of the city, which signals how central bathing was to public life. The men’s section contains a sequence of rooms arranged around a central corridor. The apodyterium has stone benches running along the walls and rows of niches in the plasterwork above — these were used to store clothing while the bather was inside. Vaulted ceilings and small windows kept the heat in. Painted stucco decoration survives on several ceilings and walls, evidence that even a functional civic building was designed to be visually impressive.

The separate women’s section of the Forum Baths is smaller, reflecting the lower priority given to women’s bathing in Roman society. Literary sources, including remarks in the Satires of Juvenal, make clear that some Romans considered mixed bathing morally problematic, though the practice did occur at certain establishments. The physical layout of the Forum Baths — two completely separate sequences of rooms — is strong material evidence for gendered segregation in Roman public life.

The Hypocaust: Roman Underfloor Heating

What made the caldarium possible was a remarkable feat of engineering: the hypocaust. A wood-burning furnace, called the praefurnium, heated the air in a hollow space beneath the floor. The floor itself rested on short pillars of brick called pilae, allowing hot air to flow freely underneath. The same hot air passed through hollow tiles built into the walls, known as tubuli, so that the room was heated from below and all around. Bathers walking on the floor of the caldarium would have felt the warmth rising through the thick tiles. In the hottest rooms, bathers commonly wore wooden-soled sandals to protect their feet. This system was efficient enough to heat large public rooms to temperatures comparable with a modern sauna.

Romans cleaned themselves differently from modern bathers. Rather than using soap, they applied scented olive oil to the skin and then scraped it off — along with the dirt — using a curved metal tool called a strigil. This was done either by a personal slave (for the wealthy) or by a specialist slave employed in the baths. The sequence typically ran: undress in the apodyterium, warm up in the tepidarium, sweat in the caldarium, be scraped and oiled, then cool down in the frigidarium or plunge into the cold pool.

Many visitors then visited the palaestra, an open exercise courtyard adjacent to the bath building. Running, wrestling, ball games and weight training all took place here. Seneca, writing to his friend Lucilius, describes the sounds of a bath complex next to his lodgings — the grunting of weightlifters, the splashing of plunges and the calls of vendors selling snacks — painting a vivid and noisy picture of bath life (Seneca, Epistulae Morales 56).

The Baths as a Social Centre

Horace, writing in his Satires, refers to his own modest bathing habits and the contrast with those who used the baths to show off expensive slaves and perfume. This reveals that the baths were a place where social differences were on display even as they were also temporarily dissolved — a senator and a freedman might be found in the same tepidarium, though their entourages and personal slaves would have made their status visible. The baths were, in this sense, one of the few genuinely public spaces in Roman city life where different social groups met face to face.

Key Fact

The baths served social and political purposes as well as hygienic ones. Local politicians and emperors sponsored free bathing days as a form of public generosity (euergetism). Controlling access to luxuries like the baths was one way the Roman elite maintained their status and popularity.

Literary sources such as Seneca’s Epistulae Morales and Horace’s Satires provide vivid personal accounts of bath life, but they represent the perspective of educated, upper-class Roman men. Seneca writes about the sounds and distractions of a noisy bath complex from the viewpoint of a writer trying to concentrate. Horace’s satire mocks those who bathe too elaborately as a social performance. Neither source tells us about the experience of ordinary workers, slaves or women.

Material evidence — the physical remains of the Forum Baths at Pompeii or the Central Baths at Herculaneum — fills some of these gaps. The layout shows us the separation of men’s and women’s sections, the scale of investment in heating systems and the quality of the decoration. However, material evidence cannot tell us how often people visited, how they felt about the experience, or the full range of social activities that took place. The strongest analysis draws on both types of source together.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Roman public baths (thermae) were a social, hygienic and political institution. Bathers followed a sequence of rooms — apodyterium, tepidarium, caldarium, frigidarium — cleaning themselves with oil and a strigil rather than soap.
  • The hypocaust, an underfloor heating system using hot air circulated beneath a raised floor, made the caldarium possible. The Forum Baths at Pompeii survive as a prescribed material source illustrating these features.
  • Literary sources such as Seneca’s Epistulae Morales and Horace’s Satires show the baths as a noisy social arena where status was both displayed and briefly dissolved. Material and literary sources together give the fullest picture of bath life.

before.content_html:
The Culture of the Arena

Of all the forms of entertainment in the Roman world, none was more spectacular or more controversial than the gladiatorial games. The munera (gladiatorial shows) were staged in purpose-built oval arenas called amphitheatres. The word ‘amphitheatre’ means ‘theatre on both sides’ in Greek — the design placed the audience all around the central fighting floor, called the arena (Latin for ‘sand’, which absorbed the blood). Games were expensive to stage and were funded by emperors, politicians and local magistrates as a public gift to the citizens — a form of political self-promotion as much as entertainment.

The Prescribed Source: The Colosseum, Rome

The most famous amphitheatre in the Roman world is the Colosseum in Rome, officially known as the Flavian Amphitheatre, begun by the Emperor Vespasian and completed under Titus in AD 80. The building is an enormous ellipse, measuring approximately 188 metres long and 156 metres wide, with an outer wall standing around 50 metres tall. The exterior is divided into four levels, the lower three decorated with arches framed by engaged columns in the three architectural orders: Tuscan on the ground floor, Ionic on the second and Corinthian on the third. The fourth level is a solid attic storey with Corinthian pilasters and corbels that supported the masts for the velarium awning.

Inside, the seating was arranged in tiers corresponding to social rank. Senators occupied the front rows, closest to the action. Behind them sat the equestrian class, then ordinary male citizens, and at the very back, in open wooden sections under a canvas awning called the velarium, sat women and the poor. This seating arrangement made the amphitheatre a visual map of Roman society. Beneath the arena floor lay a complex of tunnels, cages and lifts called the hypogeum, through which animals and fighters could be raised dramatically into the arena through trapdoors.

Key Fact

The Colosseum could hold an estimated 50,000 spectators. Its 76 numbered entrances (vomitoria) allowed the audience to fill and empty efficiently. The seating tiers reflected Roman social hierarchy: senators at the front, women and the poor at the back under the velarium.

Types of Gladiator

Gladiators were not a single type. Different categories of fighter were recognised by their equipment, fighting style and the opponents they typically faced. The major types to know are:

The murmillo carried a large rectangular or oval shield and wore a distinctive helmet decorated with a fish crest. His main weapon was the short sword, the gladius. He typically fought against the retiarius. The retiarius was almost the opposite: lightly protected, he wore only an arm guard (manica) and shoulder piece (galerus), and fought with a weighted net to entangle his opponent and a trident to finish the fight. The contrast between the heavy murmillo and the nimble retiarius made for dramatic theatre. The thraex used a short curved sword called a sica and carried a small rectangular shield, fighting in a style associated with the peoples of Thrace.

Gladiatorial combat was not the only form of entertainment in the amphitheatre. The morning programme typically featured venationes — hunts in which specially trained fighters called venatores fought wild animals such as lions, bears, leopards and elephants imported from across the empire. These hunts both entertained the crowd and demonstrated the reach of Roman power: controlling exotic animals from distant lands was itself a symbol of imperial strength.

The midday slot was sometimes given over to public executions (damnatio ad bestias), in which condemned criminals were exposed to animals. This combination of entertainment and public justice was viewed differently by Roman and modern audiences. Some Romans, such as the philosopher Seneca, expressed unease at the brutalising effect of such spectacles on the audience, while others saw them as a legitimate expression of Roman order and power.

Roman Attitudes to the Spectacle

Modern audiences often assume that Romans uniformly celebrated the bloodshed of the arena. The reality was more complex. Juvenal, writing in his Satires, used the phrase ‘bread and circuses’ (panem et circenses) to mock what he saw as the debasement of Roman citizens who no longer cared about politics, only about food and entertainment. This suggests that not all educated Romans viewed the games uncritically. Seneca, in one of his letters, writes that he attended the midday shows and came away feeling he had lost something of himself from watching the violence — a striking personal critique of the culture of spectacle.

Key Fact

Gladiatorial games (munera) were organised and paid for by editors. The emperor was the most important editor, and shows staged at the Colosseum by emperors were political events as much as entertainment. A generous editor won popularity; a poor show risked booing and public embarrassment.

There is a common misconception that all gladiators were unwilling slaves fighting to the death at every show. The reality was more nuanced. Gladiators did include slaves and criminals sentenced to fight, but there were also free volunteers (auctorati) who signed contracts with gladiatorial schools (ludi) in exchange for money, training, food and accommodation. A successful gladiator could earn substantial prizes and, if he survived long enough, a symbolic wooden sword (rudis) signifying his honourable discharge.

Combat was not automatically to the death. A defeated gladiator who had fought well could appeal to the crowd and the editor by raising his left hand (missus). The crowd’s response — waving cloths if they wanted him spared, turning thumbs if not (though the exact gesture is debated by historians) — influenced but did not always determine the outcome. The editor made the final decision. Killing a well-trained gladiator unnecessarily was costly; keeping him alive meant he could fight again.

before.content_html:
Roman Theatre

The Romans inherited theatre from the Greeks, but adapted it to their own tastes and social context. Roman theatre buildings differed from Greek ones in important ways: Greek theatres were cut into hillsides to use natural slopes for seating, while Roman theatres were freestanding stone structures built on level ground, using arched substructure to support the tiers. The seating area (cavea) was a semicircle rather than the more-than-semicircle of Greek theatres, and the stage building (scaenae frons) was an elaborate multi-storey stone backdrop decorated with columns, niches and statues. The stage itself was lower and wider than its Greek predecessor. Roman theatres in the prescribed sources include the large theatre at Pompeii, which was built into the slope of a hill and could seat an estimated 5,000 spectators.

The Large Theatre at Pompeii

The large theatre at Pompeii is a prescribed material source. Built in the second century BC and remodelled in the Augustan period, it is one of the oldest surviving examples of a Roman theatre. Its form combines elements of both Greek and Roman design. The cavea is cut partly into the slope of a hill (mons) and partly supported by arched substructure, giving it a transitional character between the purely Greek hillside theatre and the purely Roman freestanding design. The stage and the scaenae frons behind it have been largely lost, but inscriptions on the theatre and tombs nearby — including the Tomb of Naevoleia Tyche — provide evidence for the people who funded and used theatrical performances. Naevoleia Tyche was a freedwoman who funded a public building and was commemorated with images of a ship and a bisellium, suggesting she or her husband had held civic office and was proud of it.

Roman drama ranged from literary comedy to popular mime. Roman comedy (comoedia) was heavily influenced by Greek New Comedy. It relied on stock characters: the cunning slave (servus callidus) who outwits his master; the boastful soldier (miles gloriosus); the miserly old man (senex); the young man in love. Performances used masks, colourful costumes and exaggerated gestures so that audience members far from the stage could follow the action.

Mime (mimus) and pantomime (pantomimus) were even more popular with Roman audiences than literary comedy. Mime was a short, often bawdy, improvised or scripted performance without masks, featuring female performers as well as male — a significant difference from Greek drama, where all roles were performed by men. Pantomime was a more refined form: a solo dancer performed narrative scenes from myth using music and gesture, while a chorus narrated. The famous Juvenal passage about pantomime performers mocking the gods (Satires 6) shows that such performances were controversial as well as popular.

Key Fact

Roman actors (and especially actresses) were legally classified as infames — people of low social standing who had forfeited normal civic rights. Yet popular performers could be idolised by audiences, causing tension with the elite. Pliny (Letters 7.24) records with disapproval that a senator was seen applauding a pantomime performer.

Chariot Racing

If the amphitheatre offered Romans violence and drama, the circus offered pure speed and the passionate tribal loyalty of the factions. Chariot racing was the oldest and arguably most popular form of public entertainment in Rome. Races were held in the circus, an oval track centred on a long narrow barrier called the spina. Chariots raced seven laps around the spina. The standard unit was one race of seven laps, and a typical day of racing might feature up to twenty-four races.

The Circus Maximus, Rome

The greatest of all Roman circuses was the Circus Maximus in Rome, a prescribed material source. Sitting in the valley between the Palatine and Aventine hills, the Circus Maximus was the largest public building in the Roman world. In its imperial form it measured around 600 metres in length and 200 metres in width, with seating capacity estimated by ancient sources at well over 100,000 spectators — modern historians suggest the figure may have reached 150,000 or more. The starting gates (carceres) occupied one curved end of the track, arranged in a staggered line to give each chariot an equal distance to the first bend. The spina in the centre was decorated with obelisks, lap-counting mechanisms (seven wooden eggs and seven bronze dolphins were moved to count the laps), and temples. The Circus Maximus was a venue for religious processions as well as races; the games often honoured specific gods, and the procession (pompa) before racing was itself a religious ceremony.

Key Fact

Charioteers and their horses competed for four colour-coded teams called factions: the Blues (Veneti), Greens (Prasini), Reds (Russati) and Whites (Albati). Support for a faction was inherited and passionate. The charioteer Gaius Appuleius Diocles, recorded in inscriptions, competed in over 4,000 races and won more than 1,400 — one of the most celebrated sporting careers in the ancient world.

Juvenal (Satires 11) describes the noise and excitement of the Circus Maximus in vivid terms, but from the perspective of a man who refuses to attend, preferring to read in peace while the rest of Rome empties into the races. His tone is one of superiority and mild contempt for the masses who are so easily swept up in faction loyalty. He contrasts the modern enthusiasm for chariot racing with what he sees as the more sober, martial values of earlier Romans.

Pliny the Younger (Letters 9.6) expresses a similar disdain. He writes to a friend confessing that he cannot understand the appeal of watching horses race round a track, when the fans care only for the colour of the cloth (the faction colours), not for the skill of the individual rider. Both sources reveal how chariot racing created an almost tribal loyalty that cut across social class — and both reveal the ambivalence of educated Romans towards this most popular form of entertainment.

Slavery at the Heart of Roman Society

Roman city life — its baths, its banquets, its great houses and its public buildings — depended on the labour of enslaved people. Slavery was not a marginal feature of the Roman world; it was embedded in every level of society. Wealthy households might own hundreds of slaves; a prosperous artisan might own two or three; and the Roman state itself owned slaves who worked in mines, on public building projects and in the administrative offices of the city. Modern scholars estimate that slaves may have made up somewhere between 20 and 35 per cent of the population of Italy during the late Republic and early Imperial period, though precise figures are impossible to establish.

A person could become a slave in several ways. The most common route in the earlier Republic was capture in war: defeated enemies were sold into slavery in enormous numbers. The children of enslaved women were born enslaved regardless of who their father was. People could also be enslaved as a punishment for certain crimes, or through debt, though debt bondage was abolished relatively early in Rome’s history. Exposure of unwanted infants — a practice that was legal in Rome — sometimes resulted in children being collected by slave traders and raised for sale.

Key Fact

Enslaved people in Roman cities performed an enormous range of tasks: domestic service (cooking, cleaning, childcare, dressing their owner), skilled trades (reading, accounting, medicine, teaching, craft work), public labour (building, roads, mines), and personal entertainment (musicians, readers, secretaries). The range of enslaved people’s roles meant that some held positions of considerable responsibility and even influence within wealthy households.

The Legal Position of Slaves

In Roman law, an enslaved person was legally defined as a res — a thing, not a person. This meant they could be bought, sold, hired out, punished and even killed by their owner, though the law eventually placed some limits on extreme cruelty. Slaves could not own property, make contracts or appear in court. Any earnings or property a slave accumulated was technically their master’s, though in practice many enslaved people were allowed to accumulate a personal fund called the peculium, which they might use to buy their freedom.

The relationship between enslaved people and their owners varied enormously. Pliny the Younger, writing in his Letters (3.14), describes being shocked and saddened by the murder of a fellow senator’s household slaves, and expresses genuine affection for his own staff. This is worth reading carefully: Pliny is an elite male writing about elites for an elite audience, and his sympathy does not challenge the institution of slavery itself. Petronius’s Satyricon presents a different perspective: the nouveau-riche freedman Trimalchio boasts at his dinner party about having once been a slave and having risen to great wealth, but his treatment of the enslaved people at his table reveals the arbitrary cruelty that underpinned even a ‘kind’ master’s power.

Romans were aware of the potential for enslaved people to resist or rebel. The slave revolt led by Spartacus (73–71 BC), in which tens of thousands of enslaved people defeated Roman armies for two years before being crushed, cast a long shadow over Roman attitudes. Pliny (Letters 3.14) reveals this anxiety when he notes that a murdered senator’s household slaves knew about the murder in advance but said nothing: the whole household could be executed under Roman law if a master was killed, as a deterrent. This practice — the collective punishment of all slaves in a household — shows both Roman anxiety about slave revolt and the legal violence that kept the system in place.

Manumission: The Path to Freedom

Manumission — the freeing of an enslaved person — was a distinctive feature of the Roman slave system. It was far more common in Rome than in most ancient societies. Owners might free slaves as a reward for long service, as a provision in their will, as an act of affection, or (cynically) to avoid having to support ageing enslaved people who were no longer economically useful. An enslaved person who saved enough from their peculium could also purchase their own freedom. Formal manumission by a Roman citizen created a new legal status: the libertus (freedman) or liberta (freedwoman) became a Roman citizen.

Key Fact

Freed slaves received Roman citizenship but faced significant restrictions. They could not stand for election to the Senate or hold major magistracies, and were expected to perform certain duties for their former owner, now called their patronus. Their children, however, faced no such restrictions and could advance fully in Roman society.

Freedmen in Roman Commerce and Society

Freedmen played a vital role in Roman commerce and administration. Because Roman aristocrats considered direct involvement in trade to be beneath their social status, they frequently ran businesses through freedmen agents who could conduct transactions on their behalf. Many freedmen became wealthy merchants, bankers, craftsmen and contractors. The most famous literary example is Trimalchio in Petronius’s Satyricon (the Cena Trimalchionis, chapters 26–78): a former slave who has accumulated enormous wealth through trade and now hosts an extravagant dinner party, surrounding himself with every luxury money can buy.

Petronius presents Trimalchio as simultaneously admirable and ridiculous — his wealth is real but his taste is vulgar, his manners are ostentatious, and his constant references to his slave origins suggest someone who has not quite escaped his past. The Satyricon is satirical fiction, so we should not read it as a straightforward historical document. Nevertheless, it tells us a great deal about Roman anxieties around social mobility: the freedman who becomes too rich, too powerful, too visible threatens the established social order.

The Tomb of Naevoleia Tyche at Pompeii is a prescribed material source that combines several of these themes. Naevoleia was a freedwoman who erected a large, elaborately decorated tomb for herself and her husband Gaius Munatius Faustus. The inscription records that she paid for public construction projects out of her own money. The carved decoration shows a ship, suggesting commercial wealth, and a bisellium — a two-seated ceremonial chair given to those who had held civic office or received public honours. A freedwoman funding public buildings and commemorating herself with the symbols of civic prestige is a striking statement about what freedmen and women could achieve, and about how they used material culture to establish their social identity.
before.exam_tip_html: Questions about slaves and freedmen often ask you to use a literary source. The key sources are Pliny (Letters 3.14 — murder of a senator’s slaves) and Petronius (Satyricon, Dinner with Trimalchio — the freedman as a social-climbing figure). When using Petronius, remember it is satirical fiction: state that it is not straightforward evidence, then explain what the satire reveals about Roman anxieties. The biggest error is to treat Petronius as a realistic account. For material source questions, the Tomb of Naevoleia Tyche is your key example of a freed person’s self-presentation. Always push from ‘what it shows’ to ‘what it reveals’ about Roman attitudes to social mobility.

practice_questions.text:
Read the following passage, which is based on Petronius's Satyricon (Dinner with Trimalchio, sections 37–38):

'Our host, as you could see, had once been a slave himself. He was not ashamed to say so. He had begun with nothing and now owned more than most men could dream of. He pointed out his silver and his paintings, his armies of slaves dressed in their best. Every dish that came to the table was an announcement of wealth, every guest a witness to his rise. Yet for all his gold, something in his manner betrayed a man still measuring himself against what he had once been.'

What does this passage suggest about the position of freedmen in Roman society? Use details from the passage in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses specific details (Trimalchio's slave origins openly acknowledged; display of silver, paintings, slaves; 'measuring himself against what he had once been') to analyse the tension between wealth and social stigma; notes the satirical purpose of Petronius and what that tells us about elite anxieties regarding social mobility; draws on wider knowledge (the restrictions on freedmen, Pliny's Letters, Naevoleia Tyche) for context.
Secure: Identifies two details from the passage and explains what they reveal about freedmen's social position.
Developing: Identifies one detail with limited explanation; may describe rather than analyse.
Emerging: Paraphrases the passage without analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain what happened when an enslaved person was freed (manumission) in Rome.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per developed point (up to 4). Points may include: freed slaves received Roman citizenship (1); they were known as liberti (freedmen) or libertae (freedwomen) (1); they faced restrictions — could not hold senatorial office, were expected to perform duties for their former owner (patronus) (1); their children faced no such restrictions and could advance fully (1); a freed slave could acquire wealth through commerce, as illustrated by Trimalchio in the Satyricon (1).

practice_questions.text: How useful is Petronius's Satyricon as evidence for the lives of enslaved people and freedmen in Rome? Refer to specific details in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Weighs value (vivid detail about a freedman's wealth, display, social anxiety; contemporary first-century AD setting; captures elite attitudes to social mobility) against limits (it is satirical fiction deliberately exaggerating for comic effect; written from an elite perspective; Trimalchio may be a comic type rather than a realistic individual). Compares with Pliny's Letters (a different type of literary source) and the Tomb of Naevoleia Tyche (material evidence that independently confirms freedmen's wealth and civic ambition). Balanced conclusion.
Secure: Identifies at least two useful elements and two limits; some reference to other sources.
Developing: Mostly describes Petronius without evaluating usefulness.
Emerging: Brief general answer.

practice_questions.text: 'The institution of slavery reveals that Roman civilisation was built on exploitation rather than values.' How far do you agree? Use evidence from literary and material sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated argument. Agrees: the legal classification of slaves as res (things), the collective punishment clause (Pliny 3.14), venationes and arena executions all reveal institutionalised exploitation. However, complicates the picture: manumission was relatively common and created genuine pathways to freedom and wealth; the Tomb of Naevoleia Tyche shows freedpeople achieving civic status; Pliny expresses genuine distress about the murder of slaves (though without questioning the system). Reaches a supported, nuanced judgement.
Secure: Addresses both sides with at least two named sources; clear argument and conclusion.
Developing: Mostly one-sided; limited evidence.
Emerging: Brief, general points with no supported judgement.

glossary_terms.definition: A thing; in Roman law, enslaved people were classified as property (res) rather than persons, meaning they had no legal standing of their own.
A sum of money or property held by an enslaved person with the informal permission of their owner, which could eventually be used to purchase their own freedom.
The legal act by which an owner freed an enslaved person in Rome, making them a freedman or freedwoman.
A formerly enslaved person (man or woman) who had been freed through manumission, holding Roman citizenship but with certain social and legal restrictions.
The former owner of a freed slave, who became their patron and to whom the freedman owed certain obligations of loyalty and service.
A funerary monument in Pompeii erected by the freedwoman Naevoleia Tyche, decorated with a ship, a bisellium (a ceremonial two-seater chair) and an inscription naming her public benefactions.

before.content_html:
Religion in Every Corner of City Life

Roman religion was not confined to temples and official ceremonies. It was woven into the texture of daily urban life in ways that would have been almost invisible to Romans because they were so routine. Every home, however humble, had a place for worship. Every street corner in Pompeii had a painted shrine. Every meal began with a small offering, and the Roman calendar was dense with festivals that punctuated the working year. Unlike many modern religious systems, Roman religion did not demand exclusive loyalty to a single deity — Romans worshipped many gods simultaneously, adding new deities to their religious world as the empire expanded. The result was a religious culture that was practical, flexible and deeply social.

Household Gods: the Lares and Penates

At the centre of domestic religion were the Lares — protective spirits tied to the family and the home. Every Roman household had its own Lares, typically depicted as young dancing figures holding drinking vessels and a libation dish. Offerings of incense, wine, cakes and garlands were made to the Lares daily, especially on the Kalends (first), Nones and Ides of each month. The Penates were a related group of deities associated specifically with the household’s food supplies and inner rooms. Together the Lares and Penates constituted the heart of Roman domestic religion.

The Genius of the paterfamilias — the spirit of the male head of the household — was also honoured at the domestic shrine. The Genius was not simply the man himself but his divine life-force, his capacity for creativity and generation. Worshipping the Genius of the paterfamilias reinforced the authority of the male head of the household within the family’s religious as well as social life.

Key Fact

The household shrine was called the lararium. In Pompeii, lararia survive in many houses — from the simplest painted wall niche in a kitchen to the elaborate freestanding marble shrine in a wealthy atrium. They typically showed the Lares flanking a central togate figure performing sacrifice, with a snake below (a protective symbol). Daily offerings and prayers at the lararium were one of the most consistent acts of Roman religious practice.

Street Shrines: the Compital Lares

The Lares were not only domestic but also public. At the crossroads (compita) of Roman streets stood shrines to the Lares Compitales — the Lares of the crossroads, protecting the neighbourhood rather than any single household. In Pompeii, the walls at many street intersections preserve painted shrines showing the Lares and the Genius of Augustus flanking a central sacrificial scene. The compital shrines were maintained by local communities, including freedmen and even enslaved people who otherwise had limited access to civic religion. Augustus reorganised the city of Rome into 265 neighbourhoods (vici), each with its own compital shrine, as a way of integrating the city’s population into a shared religious and civic identity.

As well as the domestic and neighbourhood shrines, Roman cities were filled with temples. The forum at Pompeii was flanked by several temples, including one to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva on the north side — the Capitolium, honouring the same triad worshipped on the Capitoline hill in Rome itself. This connection was deliberate: Roman cities reproduced the sacred topography of Rome as a way of declaring their Roman identity. Beyond the forum, temples to Isis, to Venus, to Apollo and to the genius loci (spirit of the place) could all be found in a city like Pompeii. The density and variety of temples shows that Roman city religion was not centralised around one deity but was genuinely pluralistic.

Public Festivals and the Religious Calendar

The Roman calendar was structured around religious festivals. There were several dozen officially recognised public festivals each year, most associated with specific deities and involving processions, sacrifices, games and feasting. The Lupercalia, held on 15 February, was one of the oldest Roman festivals: two groups of young priests (Luperci) ran nearly naked through the streets of Rome after sacrificing a goat and a dog, striking women they passed with strips of the animals’ skins (februa) in a rite associated with purification and fertility.

The Saturnalia, held in the week around 17 December, was perhaps the most beloved festival in the Roman world — a period of feasting, gift-giving and a remarkable temporary reversal of normal social roles in which masters served their slaves at table. Horace’s Satires (2.7) mentions the Saturnalia as a time of relaxed rules and indulgence — a poem in which the slave Davus uses the Saturnalian licence to speak freely to his master. The festival honoured Saturn, the god of agriculture and an earlier age of equality, and for several days the normal hierarchy of Roman society was symbolically inverted, though the institution of slavery remained entirely intact.

Key Fact

Both the Lupercalia and the Saturnalia are prescribed festivals for this unit. The Lupercalia involved ritual purification and striking with goat-skin strips; the Saturnalia involved role reversal (masters serving slaves), gift-giving and feasting. Both reveal how Roman religion served social functions beyond the purely religious: the Saturnalia temporarily relieved social tension, while the Lupercalia connected the city to ancient rites of purification and fertility.

Horace’s Satires give passing but vivid glimpses of Roman religious practice woven into everyday life — the Saturnalia as a time of feast and relaxation, the countryside shrines honoured as a traveller passes. These are not formal theological statements; they show religion as a natural part of Horace’s world rather than something he thinks about consciously. The incidental nature of these references is itself significant: it suggests religious practice was so ordinary that no explanation was needed.

Pliny the Younger, in Letters 1.9, describes how the baths and the city create an overwhelming noise that prevents him from thinking. His letter touches on the way public life — baths, games, festivals — consumed the Roman day, leaving little space for private reflection. Read against the material evidence of Pompeian lararia and compital shrines, this literary evidence helps us reconstruct a Roman city in which public and private religion were both constant and inseparable from other aspects of daily life.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Roman domestic religion centred on the Lares and Penates, worshipped at the household shrine (lararium). Lararia survive in many Pompeian houses, from kitchen niches to elaborate marble shrines. Street shrines to the Lares Compitales extended this worship to the neighbourhood level.
  • The Roman religious calendar included prescribed festivals such as the Lupercalia (purification, fertility, mid-February) and the Saturnalia (feasting, gift-giving, role reversal, mid-December). Both festivals served social as well as religious functions.
  • Literary evidence from Horace’s Satires and Pliny’s Letters shows religion as inseparable from everyday Roman city life — incidental but constant. Material evidence from Pompeii (lararia, compital shrines, temples) confirms this picture of a dense and pluralistic religious culture.
